messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thanh is a 60-year-old Vietnamese-American man who has managed a mid-sized hotel in the Pacific Northwest for nearly two decades. He lives with his long-term partner and was, by all accounts, a steady and capable professional — the kind of man who prided himself on knowing every corner of his building and keeping things running without incident. That self-image collapsed approximately fourteen months ago when a contractor improperly stored and mixed industrial cleaning chemicals in a poorly ventilated basement utility room. Thanh, conducting his customary morning walkthrough, entered the room and within seconds felt a searing burn in his throat and nasal passages, his eyes streaming, his chest tightening as if gripped from the inside. He stumbled backward into the corridor, unable to call out, certain in those moments that his lungs were being destroyed. Emergency services were called; he was hospitalised overnight for chemical inhalation injury. The physical damage was assessed as moderate and largely resolved within weeks. What did not resolve was everything else.

In the months that followed, the memory of those moments in the utility room began returning in a form that felt nothing like ordinary recollection. Without warning — during a staff briefing, while reviewing invoices, while simply walking the hotel's corridors — the memory would force itself into Thanh's mind with an immediacy that erased the present. He would feel the burn again at the back of his throat, and, most disturbingly, he could taste it: a sharp, acrid chemical taste that arrived with the memory as though it were still happening. He has described these intrusions as not remembering but returning — the sensation that fourteen months had collapsed and he was once again in that room, unable to breathe, certain he was dying. These intrusive episodes, in their vividness and bodily immediacy, reinforced his deepest fear: that his body had been permanently altered and could no longer be trusted. The taste arriving unbidden felt like evidence that something was still wrong inside him, and this conviction — that his body was unreliable — deepened each time the memory broke through.

That belief became the lens through which Thanh interpreted almost every physical sensation. He had come to feel that he could not stop bad things from happening to him, that the exposure had confirmed a fundamental helplessness he could no longer argue against. These appraisals did not remain abstract; they drove his behaviour in ways that accumulated into a recognisable pattern. He began scanning his body constantly — attending to his breathing, monitoring the back of his throat for any trace of that chemical taste, cataloguing every tightness in his chest. He also began scanning his environment with the same vigilance, checking ventilation grates, noting the smell of cleaning products, pausing at closed doors. At work, this meant that a job requiring confident, fluid movement through the hotel had become an exercise in managed dread. He would hesitate before entering storage rooms, sometimes sending junior staff ahead. Colleagues noticed. His partner noticed. Thanh, who had once moved through the building with proprietary ease, now felt like a stranger in it — a man who no longer belonged anywhere, not in his workplace, not in the body he had inhabited for sixty years.

The vigilance itself fed the very processes it was meant to contain. When Thanh scanned his body and found a sensation — a tightness, a mild throat-clearing — his nervous system treated it as confirmation of threat, flooding him with the readiness he could not turn off. His body felt perpetually braced. When a maintenance request took longer than expected to be fulfilled, he was certain something had gone wrong, that another exposure was unfolding somewhere in the building. This state of constant physiological alert made him more susceptible to the intrusive memories, which arrived with greater force when his arousal was already elevated, and each intrusion renewed his certainty that he was helpless and his body unreliable, closing the loop tightly around him.

What finally brought Thanh to seek help was a conversation with his partner, who told him quietly one evening that she was frightened — not of anything external, but of watching him disappear into himself. He came to the first session hoping, above everything, that someone could tell him his body was not still poisoned. What he feared most was that it was.
